A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Latent Stochastic Interpolants. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering and layout changes.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original ImageNet generation results, FID comparisons, computational costs and ablations. The main text and appendices also contain generated samples and inversion examples.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and additionally reports a Gaussian-mixture prior result, sampling throughput and qualitative findings from encoder-scale and compression experiments.

M1.justification: V2 introduces an optional learnable-prior formulation, specifying gradients through prior samples and initial-KL regularization when the initial distributions differ. Appendix N also specifies an encoder-dependent Gaussian-mixture prior with stopped gradients. The original encoder/decoder architecture, InterpFlow parameterization and samplers are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ImageNet 2012 generation at 64×64, 128×128 and 256×256, with the same guidance and inversion scenarios. The added prior and compression variants concern model configurations within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands comparator membership through Table 5, adding SiD2, PaGoDA, DisCo-Diff, VDM++, SiD, RIN, CDM and ADM alongside LSI. These are cited reference FIDs with differing model sizes, FLOPs and function-evaluation counts, rather than matched experimental reruns. The original observation-space SI and internal comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The retained experiments keep their preprocessing, FID evaluation, training budgets and default 300-step deterministic sampling. Newly reported evaluations include 2×/4× compression variants and 100-step throughput measurements. Appendix N states that the new mixture-prior experiment required approximately three times more steps, conflicting with Table 4's 1K-epoch heading.

E4.justification: Table 4 extends prior sensitivity testing with a Gaussian mixture. Appendices N and P newly report instability without stopped prior gradients, qualitative normalization/tanh ablations and compression-ratio tradeoffs. The existing loss-weight, encoder-noise, parameterization and capacity-shift analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix Q newly warns that the reported sampling speeds exhibit high variance. This is qualitative uncertainty reporting only; neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, numerical uncertainty estimates or significance tests for the reported experimental results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the original Table 4 rows retain their values. V2 adds mixture-prior FID 4.26, throughput results, reference FIDs and qualitative ablation findings. It corrects the stated 100-step FLOP reductions from 73.6% to 29.7% at 128×128 and from 48.6% to 64.9% at 256×256, agreeing with unchanged Table 1 costs. These are additions and corrections, not improved scores for the retained LSI experiments.

T1.justification: V1's ELBO assumes a shared initial distribution and refers readers to Li et al. for proof. V2 generalizes it to distinct initial distributions with an initial-density-ratio term. New Appendix A provides path-space KL and ELBO theorems and proofs, while Appendix B derives an observation-space likelihood bound through the data-processing inequality. The original mathematical appendices are retained under new labels.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: joint encoder/decoder/latent-SI learning, a continuous-time ELBO, simulation-free training, flexible priors and computationally cheaper sampling. The added theory and experiments principally support these existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains encoder-scale growth as a shortcut that makes denoising easier and discusses the reconstruction-versus-computation tradeoff from compression. It adds qualifications about mixture-prior training instability, hardware-dependent throughput and the limited comparability of Table 5's heterogeneous models.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the Gaussian decoder and resulting L2 loss, and documents mixture-prior construction using per-image components, standard deviation 0.1, shuffled encodings and stopped gradients. It also explicitly states the default 3× dimensionality reduction. Encoder normalization/tanh and the TPU training setup were already documented in v1.

R1.justification: V2 adds Theodorou (2015) for the stochastic-control connection and six works supporting the new reference baselines. Appendix R provides additional comparison context, while the main positioning relative to diffusion models, latent-variable models and continuous-time generative methods remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized explanatory rewrites, expands the appendix organization, and adds acknowledgments, reproducibility and LLM-use statements. Author affiliation information also changes. The main eight-section narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adopts ICLR conference headers and typography, reflows figures and tables, expands Table 4 and adds Table 5. Figures 1–7 retain their plots, architecture diagram and sample content; the visual changes are primarily formatting and placement.

improvement.justification: The added proofs and explicit initial-prior KL treatment make the theoretical basis easier to assess, while corrected FLOP reductions resolve a numerical inconsistency with Table 1. Additional implementation explanations, ablation findings and comparison context improve transparency. The gains remain limited: the main controlled results are unchanged, the mixture experiment's longer budget conflicts with Table 4's heading, and Table 5 does not provide a controlled comparison.
